script.spoken: Squeaky disc brakes come down to three causes. By the end of this video you'll know which one you have, and you'll fix it at home with basic tools.
script.b_roll: Cold open on a close-up of the rotor squealing as the wheel spins (the thumbnail shot), then cut to me at the stand
script.pattern_change: cold open on the sound, then a cut to camera

script.spoken: Here's the ten-second test. Lift the wheel, spin it and squeeze the lever gently. A squeal that pulses once a turn points to the rotor. A steady squeal points to the pads.
script.b_roll: Overhead shot of the hand on the lever, wheel spinning

script.spoken: The cause we see most often gets fixed in the cleaning step, and you need only the four things on screen next. Glazed pads come last.
script.b_roll: Quick cuts of the three fixes, one second each
script.on_screen_text: Coming up: clean, align, bed in

script.spoken: You need isopropyl alcohol, a clean rag, the key for your caliper bolts, usually a five millimetre hex or a T25 Torx, and some fine sandpaper.
script.b_roll: Tools laid out on the bench
script.on_screen_text: Alcohol, rag, 5 mm hex or T25, fine sandpaper

script.chapter: How to fix squeaky disc brakes: clean the rotor and pads
script.spoken: Take the wheel out and pull the pads from the caliper. Look at them in good light. Dark shiny patches or a wet look mean oil or grease has got in, and across the 40 or so bikes we service each week, that's the cause of most squeals.
script.b_roll: Close-up of the pads coming out, then both pads held to the light

script.spoken: Spray alcohol on the rag, never straight on the rotor, and wipe the braking surface all the way round. Do it twice with a clean part of the rag. Don't touch the surface with your fingers afterwards.
script.b_roll: Wiping the rotor, the rag turning grey
script.on_screen_text: Alcohol on the rag, not the rotor
script.pattern_change: rag close-up and a timer graphic

script.spoken: Now lay the sandpaper on a flat surface and rub each pad in a figure of eight until the shine is gone. If the pads are soaked through, don't sand them. Replace them instead.
script.b_roll: Pad moving in a figure of eight on sandpaper
script.on_screen_text: Figure of eight until the shine is gone

script.spoken: Refit the pads and the wheel, and do the ten-second test again. Contamination is behind most of the squeals we see, so this is often where the noise stops.
script.b_roll: Spin and squeeze test, quiet this time
script.on_screen_text: Quiet? You're done. Still noisy? Keep going.
script.pattern_change: split screen: before and after audio

script.chapter: Bike brakes squeaking? Align the caliper
script.spoken: If it still squeals, the caliper may sit at an angle to the rotor. Loosen the two mounting bolts just enough that the caliper can slide sideways.
script.b_roll: Key on the two caliper bolts

script.spoken: Squeeze the brake lever hard and hold it. That pulls the caliper square to the rotor. While you hold it, tighten each bolt a little at a time, swapping between them.
script.b_roll: Hand squeezing the lever, bolts tightened in turn
script.pattern_change: two-camera cut between lever and bolts

script.spoken: Spin the wheel and look through the caliper slot. You want an even gap on both sides of the rotor. That even gap is what stops the rub and the squeal.
script.b_roll: Shot through the caliper slot with light behind it

script.spoken: If it still makes noise after that, the last fix is for pads that were never bedded in, and it's right after this.
script.b_roll: Me at the stand, the new pads on the bench

script.spoken: This part of the video is sponsored by Brindlecog Tools. Those caliper bolts need the right torque, and the Brindlecog TW-15 torque wrench covers 2 to 15 newton metres, the range brake bolts need. It clicks at the torque you set, so the bolts are tight without stripping the threads. You get 15% off with the code QUILLMERE at brindlecog dot example. Now, back to that last fix.
script.b_roll: The TW-15 on the caliper bolts, the click shown in a close-up
script.on_screen_text: Sponsored by Brindlecog Tools. Code QUILLMERE: 15% off

script.spoken: Pads that have never been bedded in, or that got hot on a long descent, can glaze over and squeal. Bedding in lays an even layer of pad material on the rotor.
script.b_roll: Rider rolling out of the shop

script.spoken: Find a flat, quiet road. Ride at a steady jogging speed and brake firmly until you're at walking pace, without locking the wheel. Do that ten times.
script.b_roll: Rider braking on a flat road, counter graphic 1 to 10
script.on_screen_text: 10 stops from jogging to walking pace

script.spoken: Then do five harder stops from a faster speed. Don't come to a full stop and hold the brake at the end, because that can leave a pad print on a hot rotor.
script.b_roll: Faster stops, rider releasing the brake at the end
script.on_screen_text: 5 harder stops. Don't hold at the end.

script.spoken: Now listen. Same bike, same road, and the squeal is gone.
script.b_roll: Silent stop on the road, then the quiet rotor in close-up

script.spoken: If your lever also feels soft, the brakes need a bleed, and that's the next video, on screen now.
script.b_roll: Me pointing at the end screen area
script.on_screen_text: Next: how to bleed hydraulic disc brakes

script.b_roll: Slow test-ride footage under the end screen elements, no new information

shorts.lines: Spin the wheel and squeeze the lever gently. Pulsing squeal, it's the rotor. Steady squeal, it's the pads. The full fix is on the channel.
shorts.closing: Loop back to the spinning wheel; related video set to the full fix

shorts.lines: Alcohol goes on the rag, not on the rotor. Wipe the braking surface twice, then keep your fingers off it. Contaminated pads and rotors cause most of the squeals we see.
shorts.closing: Ends on the quiet spin test; related video set to the full fix

shorts.lines: Loosen the two caliper bolts. Squeeze the lever hard and hold it, then tighten the bolts in turns. Check for an even gap on both sides.
shorts.closing: Ends on the even gap through the slot; related video set to the full fix
